notes.meaning: Joseph receives word that his elderly father Jacob has fallen sick. He immediately sets out to visit him, taking along his two teenage sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. Joseph wants his boys to see their dying grandfather and receive his parting blessing.

Jacob is told that Joseph has arrived to see him. Though weak and near death, he rallies his remaining strength and sits up in bed. He gathers his energy because he is about to act as the spiritual leader of God's covenant family.

Jacob begins by recounting how God Almighty appeared to him at Luz, also known as Bethel, in the land of Canaan. God met him there years earlier and gave him a solemn promise of blessing. Jacob grounds everything he is about to do in God's revealed word rather than his own wishes.

Jacob recalls God's promise to make him fruitful, multiply his descendants into a community of nations, and give them the land of Canaan as an everlasting possession. By repeating these words, Jacob reminds Joseph that their true future belongs to the promised land, not to the wealth and power of Egypt.

Jacob officially adopts Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, declaring they will count as his own direct heirs just like Reuben and Simeon. This gives Joseph a double portion of the family inheritance, the right originally belonging to the firstborn son. As a result, Joseph's sons each become founders of full tribes in Israel.

Jacob adds that any further children Joseph might have will remain under Joseph's own name. Those younger children would receive their inheritance within the territories of Ephraim and Manasseh rather than starting tribes of their own. Jacob limits the honor of full tribal headship to these two older grandsons.

Jacob looks back with tender sorrow to the death of Joseph's mother, Rachel, who died on the road to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. Because Rachel died young, she bore Jacob only two sons. Jacob honors her memory and his deep love for her by elevating her grandsons to equal status with his own sons.

Jacob notices two figures standing near Joseph and asks who they are. Because his eyesight has grown dim with old age, he cannot clearly distinguish their faces. His question also serves as the formal opening of the blessing ceremony.

Joseph replies that they are the sons God graciously gave him in Egypt. Jacob then asks Joseph to bring them close so he can place God's blessing on them. Joseph humbly credits God for his family, and Jacob prepares to pass on the covenant promises.

Jacob's eyes are heavy with old age, leaving him unable to see clearly. Joseph leads the young men close to the bed, and Jacob kisses and embraces them with deep grandfatherly love. Though physically blind like his father Isaac before him, Jacob remains spiritually alert.

Jacob marvels that he never expected to see Joseph alive again after mourning him for decades, yet God has let him see Joseph's children as well. God's generosity had completely outdone Jacob's darkest fears and brightest hopes. Recognizing God's hand in our blessings makes them all the sweeter.

Joseph steps in and moves the two youths back from Jacob's knees, then bows with his face to the ground. He shows profound reverence for his father and for the sacred blessing about to take place. Joseph positions his sons so Jacob can lay his hands upon them with ease.

Joseph arranges his sons carefully so that the older son, Manasseh, faces Jacob's right hand and the younger, Ephraim, faces his left hand. In ancient culture, the right hand was the symbol of highest favor and strength, reserved for the firstborn. Joseph expects the traditional order of birth to guide the blessing.

Jacob deliberately crosses his arms, stretching his right hand over to rest on Ephraim, the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh, the firstborn. This is the first time the Bible describes laying on hands to confer a blessing. Jacob acts with clear intention, guided by God's Spirit rather than human custom.

Jacob blesses Joseph by invoking the God before whom his fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, and the God who had shepherded Jacob all his life. This is the very first time in Scripture that God is described as a shepherd to His people. Jacob acknowledges that God has faithfully fed, guided, and protected him every day of his life.

Jacob prays that the Angel who redeemed him from all harm will bless the two young men. He asks that his name and the names of Abraham and Isaac be carried on through them, and that they multiply greatly across the land. Christian readers have long understood this redeeming Angel to be the Lord Himself, the pre-incarnate Christ who delivers His people from all evil.

Joseph is displeased when he sees his father's right hand resting on the younger brother's head. He takes hold of Jacob's hand to shift it over onto Manasseh. Joseph assumes his visually impaired father has simply made a mistake about which son was which.

Joseph speaks up directly, telling his father that Manasseh is the firstborn and should have the right hand placed on his head. He tries to steer the blessing back toward the standard rule of the oldest son receiving first rank. Joseph looks at natural birth order, but God's plan is working on a different principle.

Jacob refuses to switch his hands, insisting that he knows full well what he is doing. He prophesies that while Manasseh will indeed become a great people, the younger brother Ephraim will become even greater and grow into a multitude of nations. History fulfilled this prophecy when Ephraim grew into the dominant northern tribe of Israel.

Jacob pronounces the blessing on both grandsons that day, setting a lasting pattern for Israel by saying, 'May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.' By naming Ephraim first, he permanently establishes the younger brother ahead of the older. This phrase became a traditional blessing that Jewish parents still pray over their sons.

Jacob tells Joseph that he is about to die, but assures him that God will remain with them and bring their family back to the land of their fathers. Jacob faces his own passing with calm assurance because God's covenant cannot fail. Even when godly parents and leaders leave this world, God's enduring presence stays with His people.

Jacob grants Joseph an extra portion of land above his brothers, described as a ridge taken from the Amorites with his sword and bow. The Hebrew word for portion is Shechem, pointing to the region where Joseph's family would later settle and where Joseph's bones were buried. Jacob speaks by faith, treating this future inheritance as an already accomplished gift.
